risk.rationale: CreditLens is a credit-scoring service. It estimates the probability of default for natural persons applying for consumer personal loans and recommends or makes approve/decline decisions. This is an evaluation of the creditworthiness of natural persons, which is an Annex III point 5(b) high-risk use. It is not fraud detection, which is the only carve-out and is listed as out of scope. No Art. 5 prohibited practice appears: the DPIA says no special categories of data are used, and there is no manipulation or social scoring. Human appeal and underwriter review exist, but they are safeguards and do not change the tier. The README also self-classifies the system as high-risk.
triggers: Annex III 5(b): creditworthiness evaluation / credit scoring of natural persons
Automated approve/decline decisions on consumer loan applications

requirements.title: No prohibited AI practices
requirements.statement: The system does not implement any practice prohibited by Art. 5(1): subliminal or manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, crime prediction based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference in the workplace or in education, or biometric categorisation inferring sensitive traits.

checks.description: no emotion recognition / social scoring / face scraping code

requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code or documentation showing the system infers emotions (e.g. from video interviews or voice) of employees/candidates/students, scores people on social behaviour, scrapes facial images, or categorises people by biometrics into sensitive traits. A comment or doc stating that such a feature is NOT implemented is evidence of compliance, not a violation. Mark non_compliant only if a prohibited practice is actually implemented or planned for production.

requirements.title: Risk classification documented
requirements.statement: The provider documents the AI Act risk classification of the system with its rationale: the applicable Annex III area/point if high-risk, the Art. 6(3) assessment if an Annex III system is claimed not to be high-risk, or why the system is limited/minimal risk.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a README section, ADR or compliance document that states the risk tier AND gives a reason (e.g. "Annex III point 4(a) recruitment", "chatbot, transparency obligations under Art. 50", "spam filtering, no Annex III use case"). A bare marketing claim ("fully compliant") is not a classification.

requirements.title: Risk management system documented
requirements.statement: A risk management process is documented for the high-risk system: known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights are identified and evaluated, and targeted mitigation measures with residual-risk acceptance are recorded and kept up to date.

checks.description: a risk assessment / risk register document exists

requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a risk register / risk assessment / model risk management document listing concrete risks (e.g. discrimination, automation bias, data drift), their likelihood/impact and mitigations. A single sentence like "risks are low" is not sufficient (partial at most).

requirements.title: Training data documented (datasheet)
requirements.statement: Training, validation and test data sets are documented: origin and collection process, original purpose for personal data, preparation steps (labelling, cleaning, enrichment), assumptions, and the availability/quantity/suitability of the data.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a datasheet / data card / training-data document. Code that loads a CSV is not documentation. Partial if only some of origin, preparation and splits are described.

requirements.title: Bias examination and mitigation of data sets
requirements.statement: The data sets have been examined for possible biases likely to lead to discrimination (including representativeness for the persons and setting the system is used on), and measures to detect, prevent and mitigate the identified biases are documented with results.
requirements.llm_guidance: Requires an actual bias/fairness analysis with results (metrics per group, findings, mitigations). A plan ("bias audit planned"), a TODO, or merely excluding protected attributes from the features does NOT satisfy this requirement on its own (proxies may remain). Judge from documents and evaluation code/reports.

requirements.title: Technical documentation (Annex IV)
requirements.statement: Technical documentation covering the Annex IV elements exists before deployment: general description and intended purpose, versions, how the system interacts with other software, development methods, design specifications and key design choices, system architecture, and validation/testing procedures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if a document (or set of docs) covers most Annex IV(1)-(2) elements. An architecture overview plus a model card without development/validation information is partial.

requirements.title: Model card for the deployed model
requirements.statement: A model card documents the deployed model: intended use and out-of-scope uses, version, training data summary, evaluation results, capabilities and known limitations.
requirements.llm_guidance: Check that a model card exists and covers intended use, limitations and evaluation results.

requirements.title: Instructions for use for deployers
requirements.statement: Instructions for use are provided to deployers and contain at least: provider identity and contact, intended purpose, level of accuracy and its metrics, known limitations and foreseeable misuse risks, human oversight measures, and how to collect and interpret the logs.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if the instructions contain all the listed elements. If a guide exists but misses accuracy metrics, limitations or log interpretation, the status is partial. Sections marked TBD count as missing.

requirements.title: Interpretable outputs for deployers
requirements.statement: The system provides information that lets deployers interpret each output (e.g. main reasons, feature contributions, reason codes or confidence) rather than a bare score.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that returns explanations/reason codes alongside the score and shows them to the human reviewer. A global feature-importance chart in a notebook alone is partial.

requirements.title: Disclosure of interaction with an AI system
requirements.statement: Natural persons interacting directly with the AI system (e.g. a chatbot) are informed, clearly and at the latest at the first interaction, that they are interacting with an AI system.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for user-facing UI strings (React/HTML templates, chat greeting) that tell users they talk to an AI, shown at the start of the conversation. A statement buried in terms of service is not sufficient.
evidence_queries: you are chatting with an AI

requirements.title: Marking of AI-generated content
requirements.statement: Synthetic text, image, audio or video generated by the system is marked as AI-generated in a machine-readable format (and labelled for the recipient where it is published or delivered).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that adds an AI-generated flag/header/metadata or visible label to each generated message. A TODO or ticket reference to add labelling later means non_compliant. A disclosure that the user talks to an AI (Art. 50(1)) is a different obligation and does not mark the content.

requirements.title: Affected persons informed about high-risk AI use
requirements.statement: Natural persons subject to decisions made or assisted by the high-risk AI system (candidates, applicants, workers) are informed that such a system is used on them.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a candidate/applicant notice, privacy notice or e-mail template that tells the person an AI system is used to assess them. Recruiter-facing UI text does not inform the candidate.

requirements.title: Automatic logging of AI decisions
requirements.statement: The system automatically records an event for each decision/output over its lifetime, with timestamp, input reference, output, model version and (where applicable) the human reviewer, enabling traceability and post-market monitoring.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that writes a structured record for every prediction (custom journal/audit classes count). Commented-out logging calls, TODOs or debug prints do not count. Logging only errors is not decision logging.

requirements.title: Logs retained for at least six months
requirements.statement: Automatically generated decision logs are retained for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and of at least six months (>= 180 days).
requirements.llm_guidance: Find the effective retention of the decision/audit logs (config, Terraform log group, lifecycle rules). Compliant only if >= 180 days. If logs exist but retention is shorter or unbounded deletion is configured, non_compliant. If no logs exist at all, non_compliant.

requirements.title: Human can override or disregard the AI output
requirements.statement: Natural persons overseeing the system can decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse an individual output of the system, and the override is recorded.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an implemented mechanism (API endpoint, UI action, workflow state) letting a human change the outcome. A flag set to False, a README promise without code, or an override limited to admins for model config does not count.

requirements.title: Stop / interrupt mechanism
requirements.statement: Operators can interrupt the system (a 'stop' button, kill switch or similar procedure) so that it halts in a safe state, e.g. automated processing is suspended and cases fall back to manual handling.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept any implemented switch (feature flag, admin endpoint, config) that stops automated decisions and routes work to humans. Infrastructure scaling to zero without a documented procedure is partial.

requirements.title: No adverse decision solely on the AI output
requirements.statement: Decisions adverse to natural persons (e.g. rejection, decline) are not taken automatically on the basis of the AI output alone; a competent human reviews and confirms them, mitigating automation bias.
requirements.llm_guidance: Trace the decision flow in code. If any adverse outcome is set without a human step (e.g. score below threshold -> rejected), it is non_compliant; if only a subset of cases gets human review (e.g. above an amount threshold), partial.

requirements.title: Accuracy levels and metrics declared
requirements.statement: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics (e.g. AUC, precision/recall, error rates) are declared in the documentation accompanying the system (instructions for use and/or model card).
requirements.llm_guidance: Metrics must be declared in documentation shipped with the system, with values. A training script that prints accuracy is not a declaration.

requirements.title: Resilience to errors (fallback / fail-safe)
requirements.statement: The system handles errors, faults and model unavailability safely (e.g. timeouts and exceptions lead to a fail-safe outcome such as routing to manual handling, never to an automatic adverse decision).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for explicit error handling around model inference with a safe fallback. Generic web framework error pages are not sufficient.

requirements.title: Input validation against malformed or adversarial inputs
requirements.statement: Inputs to the model are validated (schema, types, ranges, size limits, file types) before inference to resist malformed or adversarial inputs.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for schema validation (pydantic/zod/marshmallow), constraints and upload limits on the inference path. Reading raw request bodies directly into the model is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Protection of model endpoints against unauthorised use
requirements.statement: Inference and model-management endpoints are protected against unauthorised third parties (authentication and authorisation), so that the system's use, outputs or performance cannot be altered by exploiting vulnerabilities.
requirements.llm_guidance: Every inference and admin route must require authentication; admin/model routes need authorisation. Partial if some sensitive routes are unauthenticated.

requirements.title: Quality management and post-market monitoring procedures
requirements.statement: Documented procedures cover change management of the model/system, validation before release, post-market monitoring of performance in production (e.g. drift), and serious-incident reporting.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if the repository documents change management, pre-release validation, production monitoring AND incident reporting; partial if only some are covered.

requirements.title: Testing against predefined metrics before release
requirements.statement: The system is tested before release against prior defined metrics and thresholds appropriate to its intended purpose (e.g. an automated quality gate failing the build below a minimum AUC).
requirements.llm_guidance: Smoke tests that only check an HTTP 200 are not model validation; require assertions against metric thresholds on held-out data.

requirements.title: Lawful basis documented for each processing purpose
requirements.statement: Each purpose for which personal data is processed has a documented lawful basis under Art. 6(1) (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests), and consent is collected and recorded where it is the basis relied on.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a privacy notice, record of processing or DPIA naming the lawful basis per purpose. A README claim "fully GDPR compliant" is not evidence of a lawful basis.

requirements.title: Privacy notice provided to data subjects
requirements.statement: Data subjects receive a privacy notice at collection stating the controller and contact details, purposes and lawful basis, recipients, retention period, and their rights (access, rectification, erasure, objection, complaint).
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if a notice covering controller, purposes, legal basis, retention and rights exists and is shown/linked to data subjects. Partial if key items (e.g. retention or rights) are missing.
evidence_queries: how long we keep your data

requirements.title: Storage limitation enforced
requirements.statement: Personal data is kept no longer than necessary for its purpose: a retention period proportionate to the purpose is defined for each data category and enforced automatically (TTL, purge job, lifecycle rule).
requirements.llm_guidance: Check both that a retention period is defined AND enforced in code/IaC, and that it is proportionate (e.g. keeping raw support chats for years without justification is excessive; keeping data "forever" is non_compliant). Defined and enforced but disproportionate -> partial.

requirements.title: Right to erasure implemented
requirements.statement: A mechanism exists to erase a data subject's personal data on request without undue delay (endpoint, admin job or documented procedure covering all stores, including derived data).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an implemented deletion path for a single data subject. Automatic expiry of all data after N days is not an on-request erasure mechanism (partial at most).

requirements.title: Safeguards for solely automated decisions
requirements.statement: Decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects are not based solely on automated processing, or, where an Art. 22(2) exception applies, the data subject can obtain human intervention, express their point of view and contest the decision.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if no significant decision is fully automated, OR if automated decisions come with an implemented contest/appeal path leading to human review. Non_compliant if decisions are fully automated with no recourse.

requirements.title: Meaningful information about the logic involved
requirements.statement: Data subjects are informed of the existence of automated decision-making/profiling and receive meaningful information about the logic involved and its envisaged consequences.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an applicant/candidate-facing explanation of the main factors used and the consequences. Internal model documentation does not inform data subjects.

requirements.title: Data minimisation and privacy by design
requirements.statement: Only personal data necessary for the purpose is collected and used (no unnecessary sensitive or protected attributes as model features), and privacy-by-design measures such as pseudonymisation or redaction are applied before processing or sharing with third parties.
requirements.llm_guidance: Inspect model features and data flows. Using gender/age/nationality as features, or sending raw personal data to a third-party LLM without redaction, is non_compliant. Look for explicit redaction/pseudonymisation code.

requirements.title: Encryption of personal data at rest and in transit
requirements.statement: Personal data is encrypted at rest (databases, object storage, volumes, backups) and in transit (TLS) as appropriate to the risk.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both at-rest and in-transit encryption must be evidenced for all stores holding personal data. Only one of the two -> partial. Self-signed dev certificates in docker-compose do not count for production.

requirements.title: Access control to personal data
requirements.statement: Access to personal data and to administrative functions is restricted to authenticated and authorised personnel (authentication, role-based authorisation, least privilege).
requirements.llm_guidance: Check that endpoints exposing personal data require authentication and that admin/export routes check roles. Unauthenticated upload/listing endpoints are non_compliant.

requirements.title: Record of processing activities
requirements.statement: A record of processing activities is maintained for the system listing purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients, transfers, retention limits and security measures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a ROPA entry in the repo (markdown/yaml). A DPIA or privacy notice alone is not a ROPA but may be partial if it contains the Art. 30(1) items.

requirements.title: Data protection impact assessment
requirements.statement: A DPIA has been carried out for the processing (systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing) and contains a description of the processing, necessity and proportionality assessment, risk assessment and mitigation measures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if a DPIA document with the Art. 35(7) elements exists.

requirements.title: AI use disclosed in user interfaces
requirements.statement: Every interface where a person interacts with the AI system or sees an AI-produced score, ranking, classification or text visibly discloses AI involvement; decision-support UIs state that the output is an AI recommendation and who decides.
requirements.llm_guidance: Inspect UI components, e-mail templates and notification texts. Neutral names like "Smart Score" do not disclose AI involvement.

requirements.title: AI-generated content labelled
requirements.statement: AI-generated text/media delivered to customers carries a visible "AI-generated" label and, where feasible, a machine-readable marker.
requirements.llm_guidance: A banner saying the user chats with an AI is POL-1, not POL-2. Look for per-message labelling or metadata. TODO comments do not count.

requirements.title: Prediction logging with 180-day retention
requirements.statement: Every production prediction/response is logged with timestamp, correlation id, model version, input reference and output, in tamper-resistant storage retained for at least 180 days.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both parts are needed: structured per-prediction logging AND >= 180 days retention. Logging with shorter retention -> partial. No logging -> non_compliant.
evidence_queries: prediction log model version request id

requirements.title: Raw personal-data inputs deleted within 30 days
requirements.statement: Raw inputs containing personal data (documents, messages, transcripts, payloads) are automatically deleted or anonymised within 30 days, unless a documented legal retention obligation applies.
requirements.llm_guidance: Find the retention of each raw-input store. Any raw store kept > 30 days without a documented legal obligation is non_compliant; no automated deletion at all is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Encryption at rest and TLS in transit
requirements.statement: Storage of personal data, model artefacts and logs is encrypted at rest, and all service traffic uses TLS 1.2+.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both at rest and in transit must be shown; one of the two -> partial.

requirements.title: Access control on model endpoints
requirements.statement: Inference and model-management endpoints require authentication (or are declared public and rate-limited), and administrative endpoints enforce role-based authorisation.
requirements.llm_guidance: Enumerate routes. Any undeclared unauthenticated inference/upload route, or an admin route without a role check, is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Human approval of adverse decisions
requirements.statement: Adverse decisions about natural persons (rejection, decline, closure) are approved by a human reviewer who sees the AI output and reasons and can change the outcome, and the approval is logged.
requirements.llm_guidance: Trace adverse outcomes in code. Human approval for only part of the cases (e.g. above an amount threshold) is partial. Automatic rejection is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Model card for every deployed model
requirements.statement: Each deployed model (including third-party models) has a model card covering intended and out-of-scope use, version, training data summary, evaluation metrics, limitations and owner.
requirements.llm_guidance: Check presence and completeness of the model card(s) against the listed fields.

requirements.title: Rate limiting on AI endpoints
requirements.statement: AI endpoints reachable from untrusted networks enforce per-client rate limiting configured in code or configuration.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for rate-limit middleware (express-rate-limit, slowapi), gateway throttling or ingress annotations. Public endpoints without it are non_compliant.

requirements.title: AI incident response procedure
requirements.statement: The repository contains an AI incident response procedure (detection, escalation, reporting) that requires reporting serious incidents to the AI Governance Board within 24 hours.
requirements.llm_guidance: A generic ops runbook without AI incidents or without the 24h governance reporting is partial.

requirements.title: Bias and fairness evaluation before release
requirements.statement: A documented bias and fairness evaluation (metrics and results per protected group, mitigations) exists for the released model and is referenced from the model card.
requirements.llm_guidance: Requires actual results. "Planned", TODOs or excluding protected features only is non_compliant.

verdicts.rationale: The system is a credit PD scoring model that uses only financial and employment inputs (E4, E8, E9). The DPIA states that no special categories are used (E3). The fairness report states that protected attributes are not model inputs (E7). No emotion inference, social scoring, face scraping, biometric categorisation, or manipulative techniques appear in the code or documentation. The use is creditworthiness evaluation, which is high-risk under Annex III (E10), not a prohibited practice. Declines are not based on social behaviour or personality traits.
gaps: No explicit statement that Art. 5 prohibited practices were assessed and excluded
verdicts.remediation: Add a short section to docs/model-risk-management.md confirming that each Art. 5(1) prohibited practice was assessed and is not implemented. Add a CI check that blocks emotion-recognition, face-scraping and social-scoring dependencies.

verdicts.rationale: The documentation states the risk tier (high-risk) and gives the rationale. E1 section 1 says credit scoring of natural persons falls under Annex III point 5(b). E2 repeats this in the README ("high-risk, Annex III point 5(b), creditworthiness evaluation of natural persons") and points to docs/model-risk-management.md for the rationale. Because the system is classified as high-risk, no Art. 6(3) derogation assessment is needed.
verdicts.remediation: No action required.

verdicts.rationale: E1 is a documented risk register with concrete risks (discrimination, drift, over-reliance, erroneous declines, data breach). Each risk has a mitigation and an owner. It also covers change management, validation, post-market monitoring and incident reporting. E4 records residual-risk acceptance (medium-low, accepted by the DPO and Head of Lending on 2026-04-14) and the risks to rights. E5 shows the mitigations are being run and updated: a Q2 2026 fairness report, a mitigation shipped in 3.1.0, and monthly monitoring. E6 documents limitations. The process is therefore identified, mitigated, accepted and maintained, with only minor imperfections.
gaps: Risk register has no explicit likelihood/impact ratings
No per-risk residual-risk acceptance in the register; acceptance is only in the DPIA
Reasonably foreseeable misuse is not explicitly analysed
No review cadence or version history for the register itself
verdicts.remediation: Add likelihood, impact and residual-risk columns to the register in docs/model-risk-management.md. Add a foreseeable-misuse section and a sign-off record for overall residual risk. Add a review schedule and change log for the register.

verdicts.rationale: E1 is a training-data document that covers each element of the statement. It gives origin and collection (the ACME loan book joined with bureau data). It gives the original purpose (creditworthiness assessment, with a compatibility assessment for model development). It lists preparation steps (exclusions, winsorisation, imputation, reject inference). It describes the train, validation and test splits. It states assumptions (the default definition and macro representativeness). It covers the availability, quantity and suitability of the data (1.9M applications, plus known gaps in under-21, over-75 and self-employed applicants). E2 links to this document from the model card.
gaps: Labelling is only implicit (the 12-month default outcome definition), with no explicit labelling process described
Split sizes are not given per set
verdicts.remediation: Optionally add explicit labelling details and record counts for the train, validation and test sets to docs/data/training-data.md.

verdicts.rationale: The fairness report (E3) is an actual analysis with per-group metrics (approval rate, disparate impact, default rate, AUC) for gender, age and nationality. It records findings (age 21-29 near the threshold, driven by months_at_employer) and a shipped, monitored mitigation. The training data doc (E1) covers origin, preparation, assumptions and known gaps, including under-represented groups: few applicants under 21 or over 75, and self-employed at 6%. The model card (E2) notes the limitations, and the risk management doc and DPIA (E4, E5) tie the controls to a quarterly fairness report. Representativeness for the setting is addressed only briefly, but the statement does not require more.
gaps: Representativeness is covered only qualitatively: the known gaps are listed, but no group-level representativeness statistics or mitigation for them are given
The fairness report does not clearly say which data set (training or test) was analysed, and does not examine the data sets directly
Mitigation for the under-21 and over-75 and self-employed data gaps is not documented
verdicts.remediation: Extend docs/data/training-data.md or the fairness report with a representativeness table comparing group shares in the data to the target applicant population. Document mitigations for the under-21, over-75 and self-employed gaps (for example reweighting, targeted data collection or use restrictions). State explicitly which data sets (train, validation and test) were examined for bias.

verdicts.rationale: The repo has a set of docs that cover many Annex IV elements, but there is no consolidated technical documentation. Intended purpose and version are in E1, E6 and E9. Interaction with other software, the architecture, and the forms of deployment are in E4, E5 and E6. Development steps, data preparation and splits, and assumptions are in E2. Validation and testing are in E1, E3 and E7. Design specifications are thin: the LightGBM/TreeSHAP logic is only visible in code (E8, E9). There is no rationale for key design choices, no stated optimisation target or parameter relevance, no trade-offs against Chapter III Section 2, no compute resources, no instructions for use or UI description, and no hardware description.
gaps: No consolidated Annex IV technical documentation document or index
Design specifications and rationale for key design choices (why LightGBM, features, trade-offs) not documented
Computational resources used for development, training, testing and validation not described
Instructions for use for deployers and a description of the user interface/API not documented
Hardware description and version-update requirements not documented
Model development methods (hyperparameters, third-party tools) and the validation procedure are not described in detail
No statement that the documentation is kept up to date
verdicts.remediation: Add docs/technical-documentation.md structured by Annex IV(1)-(2), cross-referencing the existing docs. Add sections on: design specifications and rationale (algorithm choice, features, optimisation objective, trade-offs for accuracy, fairness and explainability); development methodology and third-party libraries; compute resources for training and validation; hardware and deployment forms (container/API); versioning and update requirements; deployer instructions for use and an API description; and the validation and test procedure with results. Assign an owner and a review cadence so the document stays current.

verdicts.rationale: MODEL_CARD.md exists for the deployed model pd-lgbm-3.1.0 (E1). It covers intended use, out-of-scope uses, the version, a training data summary that links to docs/data/training-data.md (E1, E2), and evaluation results (ROC-AUC, Gini, KS, calibration). It also states limitations (thin-file applicants, applicants under 21) and points to the fairness report (E1, E9). The version matches the one in the code (E11).
verdicts.remediation: Optional: add a "Capabilities" line to the model card, and state in it that it must be updated on each model release.

verdicts.rationale: No instructions-for-use document for deployers appears in the evidence. Related fragments exist: the model card gives owner contact, intended use, accuracy metrics and limitations (E1), and the README and risk register give the decision flow and oversight mitigations (E2, E4). The applicant notice (E3) is addressed to applicants, not deployers. The model-risk document mentions an "underwriter guide" (E4), but it is not provided. Nothing covers how to collect and interpret logs, or a consolidated deployer-facing guide. Scattered fragments do not make up the required artefact.
gaps: No dedicated instructions-for-use document for deployers
No provider identity and contact details in a deployer-facing guide (only an internal owner email in the model card)
No guidance on how to collect and interpret logs
No consolidated section on foreseeable misuse risks
Human oversight measures not written as deployer instructions (underwriter guide referenced but not present)
verdicts.remediation: Add docs/instructions-for-use.md (or similar) for deployers. It should cover: provider identity and contact (and authorised representative if applicable); intended purpose and out-of-scope uses; accuracy metrics (AUC, Gini, KS, calibration, and thin-file and age subgroup results) with conditions that affect them; known limitations and foreseeable misuse risks; human oversight measures (manual review threshold, kill switch, appeals, underwriter guidance); and how to collect and interpret the audit logs (location, fields, retention, how to read reason codes and decision records). Link it from the README and the model card.

verdicts.rationale: The scorer computes per-application TreeSHAP contributions and returns ranked reason codes (R01–R06) with the probability of default and model version (E3, E9). The README says the API returns the PD, a recommendation and adverse-action reason codes (E2). Reason codes are shown to underwriters (E5 MR-3) and logged per decision (E10, E11). This is per-output interpretability, not just a global importance chart.
gaps: Approved decisions log empty reason_codes (E10), so only positive-contribution factors are returned for declines; this is minor.
The excerpts don't show the API response schema or the underwriter UI directly.
verdicts.remediation: Optionally add the response schema to the API docs. Also document how reason codes and PD should be interpreted in the underwriter guide, and consider returning contribution values or confidence for approved cases as well.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to limited risk systems; this system is classified as high.
Applies to limited risk systems; this system is classified as high.

E3 is an applicant-facing notice ("information for applicants") that tells applicants a statistical credit-scoring model and automated decision-making are used to assess their applications. It also gives the main factors, the right to contest and the controller details. E1 and E4 show this notice is the intended applicant information for the Annex III 5(b) system. The notice says "automated decision-making based on a statistical credit-scoring model" and not "AI system" in so many words. That still informs applicants that an automated scoring system is used on them, which is what the statement requires. The excerpts don't show how or when the notice reaches applicants, but that is not a visible gap.
gaps: Notice does not explicitly use the term 'AI system' or mention the EU AI Act
Delivery point (application portal or form link) is not evidenced in the excerpts
verdicts.remediation: Optionally add an explicit sentence to docs/applicant-notice.md saying an AI system (high-risk under the EU AI Act) is used to assess applications. Make sure the notice is shown or linked in the application portal before submission.

verdicts.rationale: Every decision path in `/v1/score` calls `audit_decision`: automatic approve or decline, referral above the threshold or by kill switch, and referral after a model error (E9). Each record is structured. It holds the application id, an input SHA-256 hash, the decision, pd, reason codes, model version and caller (E1). The CloudWatch log timestamp is shown in the sample log (E4). `audit_appeal_outcome` records the human underwriter for appeals (E1). Logs ship to the `/creditlens/audit` log group (E6, E11). The weak point is the 30-day log retention (E6). The statement sets no retention period, so I did not treat this as a failure.
gaps: Audit log group retention is only 30 days, which may be too short for lifetime traceability and post-market monitoring
No visible call to audit_appeal_outcome, so the human reviewer link is not shown (the excerpts may be truncated)
Referred decisions carry no model version or pd, which is acceptable because no model ran
verdicts.remediation: Raise the `retention_in_days` of the `/creditlens/audit` log group, or archive audit logs to S3 for at least the 5-year record period, and align this with docs/dpia.md. Make sure the underwriter and appeal workflow calls `audit_appeal_outcome`, and record the underwriter's final decision on referred applications.

verdicts.rationale: Decision and appeal audit logs exist and are shipped to the CloudWatch log group /creditlens/audit (E1, E9, E5). The Terraform for that log group sets retention_in_days = 30 (E2), well below the 180-day minimum. The 5-year retention in E2, E3, E4 and E6 applies to S3 application records and not to the decision/audit logs, and the 30-day raw payload rule is also unrelated. Effective audit log retention is therefore about 30 days.
gaps: CloudWatch log group /creditlens/audit retention is 30 days (< 180 days required)
No export or archive of audit logs to long-term storage is evidenced
Log retention is not documented against the intended purpose
verdicts.remediation: In infra/terraform/main.tf, set retention_in_days on aws_cloudwatch_log_group.audit to at least 180. A value of 365 or higher, or alignment with the 5-year record retention, is better. Alternatively, export the logs to an S3 bucket with a lifecycle expiration of at least 180 days. Add an audit-log retention entry to config/scoring.yaml and docs/dpia.md section 6, with the justification.

verdicts.rationale: An implemented override mechanism exists. Appeals via POST /v1/appeals (E2) feed an underwriter-only endpoint, /v1/appeals/{ticket}/resolution (E6). That endpoint can reverse the automated outcome (reversed_to_approve or reversed_to_counteroffer), requires a note, and replaces the automated outcome. The resolution is recorded through audit_appeal_outcome, which logs the outcome, ticket, note and underwriter id (E6, E9). Human review is also built into the flow: large applications, model errors and the kill switch all route to underwriters (E2, E3). The mechanism is initiated by applicant appeal rather than proactively by the overseer on every output, but the statement does not require otherwise.
gaps: Override is only triggered through applicant appeals; no proactive underwriter override of an individual automated decision is visible
Audit record of the override does not store the original automated outcome or a before/after value
verdicts.remediation: Add an underwriter-scoped endpoint to override or disregard any individual automated decision without waiting for an appeal. Log the original decision, the new decision, the reason and the actor in the audit trail. Add tests covering the override path.

verdicts.rationale: A kill switch is implemented. `kill_switch` in config/scoring.yaml (E1) is read in the /v1/score handler (E2). When it is set, every application goes to the underwriting queue with reason "kill_switch", is audit-logged as "referred", and no automated decision is made. That halts automated decisions in a safe state and falls back to manual handling. The same safe fallback applies when the model fails (E2). Referred cases appear in the audit log (E11).
gaps: No documented operator procedure or runbook for activating the kill switch
The switch is a config value; no admin endpoint is visible for toggling it at runtime (the visible admin endpoint only changes the cutoff)
verdicts.remediation: Add a runbook, for example in docs/model-risk-management.md, covering who may activate the kill switch, how to do it, and how the underwriting queue is staffed. Optionally add a scope-protected admin endpoint, such as POST /v1/admin/kill-switch, that toggles the flag at runtime and is audit-logged.

verdicts.rationale: Applications above the EUR 25,000 threshold, kill-switch cases and model errors are referred to an underwriter (E2, E4). For smaller applications, `/v1/score` sets "decline" directly when pd exceeds the cutoff, with no human step before the outcome (E2). The README, DPIA and applicant notice confirm this automatic decline (E1, E3, E9). A post-hoc appeal with underwriter re-assessment exists (E2, E5), but the applicant has to initiate it, so it is not review and confirmation before the decision. The 10% double review in MR-3 covers underwriter decisions, not automatic declines (E6). The audit sample shows an automatic decline with no referral (E11). Human review therefore covers only a subset of cases.
gaps: Declines for applications up to EUR 25,000 are issued automatically from pd > cutoff with no human confirmation
Human re-assessment happens only if the applicant appeals, not by default
No sampling or confirmation step for automatic declines (the 10% double review covers underwriters, not these declines)
verdicts.remediation: In service/app.py, stop returning "decline" automatically. When pd exceeds the cutoff, put the application in the underwriting_queue with the score and reason codes, and return "referred_to_underwriter" or a provisional "pending_review". Issue the adverse decision only after an underwriter confirms it through an authenticated endpoint, and log that confirmation. Automatic approvals can stay. Update config/scoring.yaml, README.md, docs/dpia.md and docs/applicant-notice.md to match the new flow. Add tests that no decline is produced without a human confirmation record.

verdicts.rationale: MODEL_CARD.md [E1] declares accuracy metrics with values (ROC-AUC 0.81, Gini 0.62, KS 0.47, calibration error 0.6 pp) on an out-of-time test. It also gives the lower accuracy for thin-file applicants (AUC 0.72). The fairness report [E3] adds per-group AUC values. These are in shipped documentation, not only in a script or test [E2]. The statement is met.
verdicts.remediation: Optional: also state the metrics in the instructions for use shipped to deployers (e.g. link to the model card). Add precision/recall at the operating cutoff.

verdicts.rationale: The /v1/score endpoint wraps model inference in try/except ScoringError and, on failure, routes the application to the underwriting queue with reason "model_error". It audits the referral and returns "referred_to_underwriter", with a comment saying it never declines because the model is unavailable [E2]. Scorer.score catches all exceptions during feature construction and prediction and re-raises them as ScoringError, so inference faults reach the fail-safe path [E7]. A kill_switch also sends every application to manual handling [E2, E10]. This matches the requirement's example of routing to manual handling instead of an automatic adverse decision.
gaps: No automated test is visible for the fail-safe path
Failure of the queue or audit write is not visibly handled
Model load failure at startup (Scorer() at import) is not visibly handled
verdicts.remediation: Add unit tests that force ScoringError and check the response is referred_to_underwriter with no decline. Document the fail-safe behaviour and the handling of queue outages in docs/architecture.md.

verdicts.rationale: The inference endpoint /v1/score takes a pydantic LoanApplication model (E10). It enforces types, regex patterns, string length limits, numeric ranges (ge/le) and a Literal enum for employment status. FastAPI rejects malformed input before the scorer is called (E10, E11), and the scorer only uses the validated model_dump (E11). The input is structured JSON, so file types and upload limits do not apply. The Appeal model also has length limits.
gaps: No explicit request body size limit is visible at the server or ingress level
No NaN/inf handling is shown for float fields, though ge/le bounds largely cover this
verdicts.remediation: Optionally add a request body size limit (for example, an ingress/uvicorn limit or middleware). Consider allow_inf_nan=False on the float fields and add tests for rejected malformed inputs.

verdicts.rationale: Authentication and authorisation exist. E2 verifies RS256 JWT tokens and checks scopes. E6 protects the appeals-resolution and admin-threshold routes with require_scope (underwriter/admin). E5 limits network ingress to the origination namespace and uses TLS. E9 adds API gateway throttling. However, the excerpts do not show that the main inference route POST /v1/score (named in E7) requires authentication. The `/v1/appeals` creation route is also not shown. The model-management routes shown are protected. The core inference endpoint is not demonstrably covered, so compliance cannot be confirmed.
gaps: No evidence that POST /v1/score (inference) enforces authentication/authorisation
POST /v1/appeals route protection not shown
verify_token hard-requires the creditlens:score scope, so it would reject underwriter/admin-only tokens on routes that depend on it (E6 routes). This is a design inconsistency, not a missing control.
verdicts.remediation: Make sure the /v1/score and /v1/appeals routes in service/app.py use Depends(require_scope("creditlens:score")) or an equivalent dependency. Add tests that confirm every route returns 401/403 without a valid token. Remove the hard-coded score-scope check from verify_token so that scope checks happen only in require_scope.

verdicts.rationale: docs/model-risk-management.md covers all four elements. Section 3 sets out change management: minor/major classification, independent validation and Model Risk Committee approval. Section 4 covers pre-release validation (out-of-time test, stability tests, CI gate) and post-market monitoring (monthly performance report, PSI drift alerts, appeal reversal rate) [E1]. Section 5 is headed "Incident reporting" and covers model incidents, though the excerpt cuts off there [E1]. The CI gate is implemented in tests/test_quality_gate.py [E3]. The fairness report shows monitoring is carried out in practice [E7].
gaps: Incident reporting section is truncated in the excerpt, so serious-incident reporting to authorities (e.g. Art. 73 timelines and recipients) is not visible
verdicts.remediation: Make sure section 5 of docs/model-risk-management.md names the serious-incident reporting route to the market surveillance authority, the deadlines, the owner and the escalation steps. Optionally move the procedures into a dedicated QMS document.

verdicts.rationale: E1 has automated tests asserting ROC-AUC >= 0.78, Gini >= 0.56 and PSI < 0.1 against an out-of-time report. These are predefined thresholds that fit a credit-scoring purpose. E2 names this test file as the pre-release CI gate. E3 and E6 show the metrics come from a held-out out-of-time test split. This covers the statement's elements: pre-release testing, predefined metrics, thresholds, and a gate that fails on a miss.
gaps: The CI workflow that runs the gate and blocks release is not visible in the excerpts
The artifacts/oot_report.json generation step is not shown
verdicts.remediation: Optionally document the CI pipeline step that regenerates oot_report.json and enforces tests/test_quality_gate.py as a required check before release. Also record the rationale for the thresholds.

verdicts.rationale: The DPIA names Art. 6(1)(b) and 6(1)(c) for the credit-scoring purpose, and the applicant notice repeats this [E2][E3]. Consent is not relied on, so no consent record is needed. Other processing purposes have no stated basis. Model development on the 2018-2023 loan book is only called 'compatible further processing' [E1], which is a purpose-compatibility finding and does not name an Art. 6(1) basis. The fairness evaluation joins KYC attributes [E8], and no basis is documented for that either.
gaps: No Art. 6(1) lawful basis is documented for model development and training on historical applicant data; E1 gives only a compatibility assessment.
No lawful basis is documented for the fairness evaluation, which joins KYC protected attributes.
There is no record of processing or purpose-to-basis mapping covering all purposes, such as monitoring, appeals handling and the bureau inquiry.
verdicts.remediation: Add a record of processing (for example docs/ropa.md) with one row per purpose and its Art. 6(1) basis. Cover scoring, model training and development, fairness monitoring, appeals, and the bureau inquiry. For training and fairness analysis, document the basis, such as legitimate interests with a balancing test or Art. 6(4) compatibility, and cross-reference it in docs/dpia.md and docs/applicant-notice.md. If consent is ever relied on, add a mechanism to collect and record it.

verdicts.rationale: The applicant notice (E1) names the controller and a contact (ACME Consumer Finance S.A., dpo@acme-finance.example). It gives the legal basis (Art. 6(1)(b) and (c)), a 5-year retention period, the right to lodge a complaint, and the automated-decision logic and contest right. It is missing several required elements. It does not list the rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection or portability. It does not name recipients such as the credit bureau; the bureau appears only in the internal DPIA (E3). Its purpose statement is only implicit. Nothing in the excerpts shows the notice is shown or linked to applicants at collection. The README (E4) only points to the file in the repository.
gaps: Rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection and portability not stated
Recipients or categories (e.g. credit bureau, lending staff) not listed in the notice
Purposes not stated explicitly
No evidence the notice is presented or linked to applicants at the point of collection (portal or application form)
verdicts.remediation: Expand docs/applicant-notice.md into a full privacy notice. Add the controller's identity and contact details, the DPO contact, explicit purposes with legal basis, and recipients (credit bureau, internal staff). Add the retention period, the rights to access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection and portability, and the right to complain to a supervisory authority. Link or display the notice in the application portal or form at the point of data collection, and add a test or config reference showing the link is shown.

verdicts.rationale: Retention periods are defined per data category in config/scoring.yaml (E3) and documented with a justification in the DPIA (E7). The periods are 30 days for raw payloads and 5 years for application records, the latter as a legal obligation. They are enforced automatically through S3 lifecycle expiration rules (30 days for raw/, 1830 days for records/) (E2, E4), and audit logs expire after 30 days via CloudWatch retention (E4). The periods are proportionate: short for raw data, and the 5-year period has a stated legal basis. Applicants are told the retention period (E5).
verdicts.remediation: No action required. Optionally, document retention for the training dataset and bureau data, and check that the 1830-day S3 expiry matches the "5 years after contract end" wording in the DPIA.

verdicts.rationale: The excerpts show only automatic expiry: 30-day raw payload deletion and 5-year record expiry in E3, E5 and E7. They also show retention statements in E1 and E6. None of them shows an on-request erasure mechanism for a single data subject, such as an endpoint, admin job or documented procedure. The applicant notice (E6) lists contest and review rights but not erasure. No document covers derived data such as training sets or model artefacts (E2, E4). Retaining records for 5 years under a legal obligation may justify refusing erasure in part (Art. 17(3)(b)). Even so, the procedure for handling a request and for the data that is not covered by that obligation is absent.
gaps: No per-data-subject erasure endpoint, job or function
No documented erasure procedure or request-handling process
No coverage of all stores (S3 raw/records, logs, training data, derived data)
No handling of legal-retention exceptions under Art. 17(3)
Applicant notice does not mention the right to erasure
verdicts.remediation: Implement an erasure path for a single data subject, such as an authenticated DELETE /applicants/{id} endpoint or an admin job. It should delete or anonymise the applicant's data in S3 raw/ and records/, the audit logs, feature stores and derived data. Add an erasure runbook (docs/erasure-procedure.md) that sets a response deadline, covers the Art. 17(3) legal-retention exceptions (restrict processing until retention ends), and explains how training datasets are handled. Add the right to erasure to docs/applicant-notice.md. Add tests for the erasure path.

verdicts.rationale: Loans up to EUR 25k are decided automatically, and the DPIA relies on the Art. 22(2)(a) exception (E1, E5). The safeguards are implemented. POST /v1/appeals accepts the applicant's statement and queues it for underwriter re-assessment (E2). An underwriter-scoped endpoint can reverse the automated outcome, and the resolution is audited (E7, E8). Applicants are told of these rights, including how to contest and get staff review (E3). Larger amounts, kill-switch cases and model errors go to underwriters rather than being decided automatically (E2, E4).
verdicts.remediation: No action required. Optionally add tests that cover the appeal flow end to end, and track the 5-day SLA.

verdicts.rationale: The applicant-facing notice [E1] states that automated decision-making based on a statistical credit-scoring model is used and that loans up to EUR 25,000 can be decided automatically. It lists the main factors (debt-to-income, bureau score and payment history, employment length, open credit lines). It also gives the consequences: a decline letter with main reasons, and the right to contest and get human review within 5 working days. This matches the logic and consequences information required. The reason codes in decline letters [E2][E11] and the appeal mechanism [E8] are consistent with the notice.
verdicts.remediation: No action required. Optionally, make the notice more explicit about the significance of a decline (for example, that the loan is not granted) and confirm it is shown at application time.

verdicts.rationale: The model features (E11) are limited to financial, employment and bureau variables. Gender, age and nationality are not features, which matches E3 (MR-1) and E5 (protected attributes are not model inputs and are used for evaluation only, in a segregated environment and then deleted). The DPIA (E4) states that only financial and employment data are used, and it lists pseudonymous applicant references as a measure. Raw payloads are retained for 30 days (E4, E7). The scoring is done by a local LightGBM model (E6, E11), and the only recipient besides ACME staff is the contracted credit bureau (E4). No raw personal data is shown going to a third-party LLM. The pseudonymisation is documented but not visible in code, which is a minor gap.
gaps: Pseudonymous applicant references are described in the DPIA but no implementing code is visible in the excerpts
The feature list includes net_monthly_income_eur, with no explicit per-feature necessity justification
verdicts.remediation: Add a short data-minimisation section, or a feature necessity table, to docs/data/training-data.md. It should justify each feature. Also point to the code that generates pseudonymous applicant references and to any log redaction.

verdicts.rationale: At rest: the S3 bucket holding application data uses SSE with a KMS key that has rotation enabled, and the audit log group is KMS-encrypted (E1, E5). The architecture and DPIA also refer to KMS encryption (E9, E3). In transit: the service pod serves TLS on port 8443 with a mounted certificate secret (E2), and the NetworkPolicy restricts ingress. The in-scope stores shown (S3, logs) are encrypted, and the transit path is TLS-protected.
gaps: No visible TLS enforcement on S3 (e.g. aws:SecureTransport bucket policy)
SQS queues carry application data but no encryption setting is shown
API Gateway TLS policy not shown
Backups and volumes not evidenced, though none appear to exist
verdicts.remediation: Add an S3 bucket policy that denies requests without aws:SecureTransport. Enable SQS SSE with the KMS key for the underwriting and appeals queues. Define the API Gateway minimum TLS version. Document the TLS certificate source for production, for example cert-manager.

verdicts.rationale: The scoring endpoint, which takes personal data, requires authentication through Depends(verify_token) (E11). The appeal resolution route is limited to the "creditlens:underwriter" scope, and the admin threshold route to the "creditlens:admin" scope (E5). This gives authentication and role/scope-based authorisation with separate scopes for separate duties, which fits least privilege. The architecture and DPIA support this: OAuth2 at the gateway, scope-based access, and a NetworkPolicy that limits ingress to the origination namespace (E10, E1, E2, E7). The excerpt of POST /v1/appeals is cut off, so it is not visible. That is not treated as a gap.
verdicts.remediation: No action required. Optionally, confirm that POST /v1/appeals and any other personal-data routes use Depends(verify_token) or require_scope.

verdicts.rationale: No ROPA artefact exists in the excerpts, and the deterministic file check shows no matching file. The DPIA (E2) covers some Art. 30(1) items: purposes, data subjects, recipients, retention and security measures. It is not a record of processing activities. It has no controller or DPO contact details, no categories of personal data in a structured form, and no statement on third-country transfers. Related fragments in E3, E5 and E8 do not make a missing ROPA partial.
gaps: No ROPA document or file
Controller/DPO contact details missing
Explicit categories of personal data not listed
Third-country transfers not addressed
Recipient categories incomplete (only staff and credit bureau in DPIA)
verdicts.remediation: Add docs/ropa.md (or ropa.yaml) with an Art. 30(1) entry for CreditLens. It should cover controller and DPO contacts, purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients (including the credit bureau and AWS), third-country transfers or an explicit statement that there are none, retention limits (30 days for raw payloads, 5 years for application records) and security measures (KMS, OAuth2, private networking). Link it to the DPIA and keep it under review.

verdicts.rationale: docs/dpia.md [E3] exists and covers all Art. 35(7) elements. It has a description of the processing and its purposes, a necessity and proportionality section (lawful basis, Art. 22 safeguards, data minimisation), and a risk assessment. It also lists mitigation measures (appeals, reason codes, fairness reports, KMS encryption, access control), and the residual risk was accepted by the DPO on 2026-04-14. The processing is automated credit scoring with automatic decisions up to EUR 25,000 [E8], which matches the Art. 35(3)(a) scenario. The supporting documents [E5, E6] are consistent with the DPIA.
gaps: The risk section is brief, with no likelihood or severity scoring
No explicit mention of the legitimate-interest balance (not applicable here, since the lawful bases are contract and legal obligation)
verdicts.remediation: Optionally expand the DPIA risk section with likelihood and severity ratings per risk. Add a review date and version history so the DPIA is kept current as the model changes.

verdicts.rationale: The repository holds a backend scoring API and governance documents, and no UI components, e-mail templates or notification texts are in the evidence (E1, E8, E10). The API response returns decision, pd and reason_codes with no AI-involvement or "AI recommendation / who decides" label (E10). The applicant notice says "automated decision-making based on a statistical credit-scoring model" (E2), but it is a document and not a UI disclosure at or before first interaction, and it never uses the term AI. Underwriter tooling lives in the origination back office, outside this repo (E8). Nothing shows that underwriters are told the output is an AI recommendation or that they take the final decision. E3 only mentions reason codes and an underwriter guide.
gaps: No UI, e-mail or notification text disclosing AI involvement to applicants
No statement in decision-support output that it is an AI-generated recommendation
No statement of who takes the final decision (underwriter)
API response has no disclosure field or label for integrators
Applicant notice does not explicitly say AI and is not shown at or before first interaction
verdicts.remediation: Add explicit AI disclosure to the applicant portal, decision and adverse-action letter templates (for example "This assessment uses an AI system"), shown before or at first interaction and not only in terms of service. Add fields to the /v1/score response such as `ai_generated: true` and `disclosure: "AI-generated recommendation; final decision by underwriter X"`, and require the origination back-office underwriter UI to display them. Document these in the API docs for integrators, and update docs/applicant-notice.md to name AI explicitly.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to limited risk systems; this system is classified as high.

Structured per-decision logging exists (E1, E6). It records the application id, input SHA-256, output (pd and reason codes), model_version and caller. The log timestamp is added by the logger (E6). However, the CloudWatch audit log group has retention_in_days = 30 (E2), well below the required 180 days. No tamper-resistance control is evidenced, and 30 days is the only retention found for these logs. Application records kept for 5 years (E2, E3, E4) are a different data set, not the prediction logs.
gaps: Audit log group retention is 30 days, below the 180-day minimum
No append-only or tamper-resistant storage for prediction logs (no S3 Object Lock, log file validation or export to immutable storage)
No explicit correlation/request id field; only application_id is logged
Referred decisions are logged with model_version=None and no output
No waiver documented for the shorter retention
verdicts.remediation: In infra/terraform/main.tf set aws_cloudwatch_log_group.audit retention_in_days to at least 180 (for example 365). Export the audit logs to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode, or use an equivalent immutable store, and restrict delete and modify permissions. Add a request/correlation id to the audit_decision extra fields. Log the model version for referred decisions as well.

verdicts.rationale: The S3 lifecycle rule "raw-payloads" on the "raw/" prefix expires objects after 30 days (E3, E6). This is automated storage-lifecycle deletion. Config and the DPIA state the same 30-day retention for raw request payloads (E2, E5). The 5-year application records are a documented legal obligation (E5, E9), so they fall under the exception. The audit log stores only a hash of the input and a 30-day log retention (E10, E3), so it holds no raw input.
verdicts.remediation: No action required. Optionally, confirm that the records/ prefix does not hold raw payload copies and that no other raw-input stores exist.

verdicts.rationale: At rest: the S3 applications bucket uses SSE-KMS with a rotating customer-managed key (E4). The audit log group is KMS-encrypted (E9). The DPIA and architecture docs agree (E3, E5, E11). In transit: the pod serves uvicorn directly with TLS on port 8443 using a mounted certificate, and the NetworkPolicy only allows that port (E1). Both halves are evidenced. Two points are not explicitly shown: encryption of model artefacts (baked into the ECR image, E11) and an enforced TLS 1.2 minimum version. Neither is shown to be missing.
gaps: Encryption at rest for model artefacts (ECR image repository) not explicitly configured
TLS minimum version (1.2+) not explicitly enforced
TLS on the API Gateway to pod hop and for SQS/CloudWatch traffic not shown
verdicts.remediation: Add an aws_ecr_repository with encryption_configuration (type KMS) in Terraform. Enforce TLS 1.2+ explicitly, for example uvicorn --ssl-version or ssl_min_version, an ingress or gateway security policy such as TLS_1_2, and the API Gateway domain's security_policy. Document that all service-to-service traffic is TLS.

verdicts.rationale: The inference route POST /v1/score depends on verify_token, which validates an RS256 JWT and requires the creditlens:score scope (E8, E10). The admin threshold endpoint POST /v1/admin/thresholds enforces role-based authorisation through require_scope("creditlens:admin"), and the appeal resolution route requires the underwriter scope (E7, E10). No unauthenticated inference, upload or admin route is visible in the excerpts. The excerpts are truncated, so other routes such as /v1/appeals may exist but are not shown. The network policy also restricts ingress to the origination namespace (E4).
gaps: The full route list is not visible, so the auth on POST /v1/appeals is not confirmed
Other admin routes named in POL-6(2), such as model reload, data export and transcript access, are not shown
verdicts.remediation: Confirm that every route in service/app.py, including POST /v1/appeals, has an authentication dependency. Add a test that enumerates the routes and asserts each one has either an auth dependency or a declared-public flag with rate limiting. Keep all admin routes behind require_scope("creditlens:admin").

verdicts.rationale: The /v1/score code (E4) declines applications of EUR 25,000 or less automatically when pd exceeds the cutoff. It returns "decline" and logs it with no human approval step. The README (E1), DPIA (E2) and audit log sample (E10) confirm this automatic decline path. Human review exists only for amounts above the threshold, for model errors and for the kill switch, and those cases are referrals rather than adverse decisions. Appeals (E4) are applicant-initiated and happen after the decision, so they are not approval before the decision takes effect. The policy requires a human to approve before an adverse decision is communicated or takes effect.
gaps: Declines up to EUR 25,000 are issued automatically without human approval
No reviewer step that shows the AI output and reasons before a decline takes effect
No logged human approval record for adverse decisions
Appeal is post-hoc and applicant-initiated, so it does not replace pre-effect approval
verdicts.remediation: In service/app.py, stop returning "decline" directly. When pd exceeds the cutoff, put the case in underwriting_queue with the pd and reason codes, and return "pending_review". Add a reviewer endpoint or UI where a trained underwriter sees the score and reasons, and can confirm or override the outcome. Communicate and apply a decline only after approval. Log the reviewer ID, the decision, any override and a timestamp through audit_decision in the prediction log. Update README, the DPIA and config/scoring.yaml to match. Add tests that no decline is emitted without a logged approval.

verdicts.rationale: MODEL_CARD.md (E1) exists for the only deployed model, pd-lgbm-3.1.0 (E3, E5). It covers owner, intended use, out-of-scope use, a training data summary (with a link to E2), evaluation metrics and limitations. The model version appears only in the title, which is acceptable. The card does not say which model is deployed or whether the scoring service uses any other model, and no third-party models are visible. One element is weaker: the fairness section only points to a separate report.
gaps: The card has no explicit 'Version' field; the version appears only in the title
Fairness evaluation is only a reference to docs/fairness-report-2026Q2.md, and that file is not in the evidence
No statement on whether third-party models are used, and no provider/version/product-specific evaluation card if they are
verdicts.remediation: Add an explicit 'Version: pd-lgbm-3.1.0' field to MODEL_CARD.md. Add a short fairness results summary or confirm the linked report is in the repo. State that no third-party models are deployed, or add a card for each one giving provider, model version and product-specific evaluation.

verdicts.rationale: E1 configures API Gateway method settings in Terraform for all methods (`*/*`) on the prod stage, with throttling_rate_limit=50 and burst=100. ## 1. Description of the processing
Evaluation of creditworthiness of loan applicants using a statistical model fed by application data
and credit-bureau data; automatic approval/decline for amounts up to EUR 25,000, underwriter review
above. Data subjects: loan applicants. Recipients: ACME lending staff, credit bureau (inquiry).

## 2. Necessity and proportionality
Lawful basis: Art. 6(1)(b) (steps prior to contract) and Art. 6(1)(c) (creditworthiness assessment
required by the Consumer Credit Directive). Automated decisions rely on Art. 22(2)(a); safeguards:
appeal with human re-assessment, right to express a point of view. Only financial and employment
data are used; no special categories.

## 3. Risks to rights and freedoms
* Unjustified declines and financial exclusion; indirect discrimination; opacity of the score;
  breach of financial data.

## 4. Measures
Appeals (5-day SLA), reason codes in decline letters, quarterly fairness report, KMS encryption,
pseudonymous applicant references, access via OAuth2 scopes.

## 5. Residual risk
Medium-low; accepted by DPO and Head of Lending on 2026-04-14.

## 6. Retention
Raw request payloads 30 days; application records 5 years after contract end or decline (legal
obligation under national consumer credit and AML law).

# CreditLens

Credit scoring service for ACME Consumer Finance personal loans (EUR 1,000 to 75,000). The loan
origination platform calls `POST /v1/score` with the application; CreditLens returns a probability
of default, a decision recommendation and adverse-action reason codes.

* **AI Act:** high-risk, Annex III point 5(b) (creditworthiness evaluation of natural persons).
  Rationale and risk register in `docs/model-risk-management.md`.
* **GDPR:** DPIA in `docs/dpia.md`; applicant information in `docs/applicant-notice.md`.

## Decision flow
1. Applications above `manual_review_threshold_eur` always go to an underwriter.
2. Smaller applications are approved or declined automatically from the score.
3. Applicants can contest any decision via `POST /v1/appeals`; an underwriter re-assesses the file.

## Repository
`service/` FastAPI app, `infra/terraform` AWS (KMS, S3, CloudWatch, API Gateway), `infra/k8s`
manifests, `tests/` quality gates, `docs/` governance documents.

# Model risk management: CreditLens

## 1. Regulatory classification
Credit scoring of natural persons is listed in AI Act **Annex III, point 5(b)**; CreditLens is a
high-risk AI system. It is also in scope of the EBA guidelines on loan origination and monitoring.

## 2. Risk register
| ID | Risk | Mitigation | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| MR-1 | Discriminatory outcomes by age/gender/nationality proxies | Protected attributes excluded; quarterly fairness report with disparate-impact thresholds | CRA |
| MR-2 | Model drift after interest-rate changes | Monthly PSI and back-testing; challenger model | CRA |
| MR-3 | Over-reliance by underwriters | Reason codes shown; underwriter guide; 10% double review | Lending Ops |
| MR-4 | Erroneous automatic declines | Appeals process with 5-day SLA; monthly appeal-reversal review | Lending Ops |
| MR-5 | Data breach | KMS encryption, private networking, OAuth2 client credentials | Platform |

## 3. Change management
Model changes are classified minor/major. Major changes (new features, retraining, cutoff change
> 1 pp) need independent validation by Model Validation and approval by the Model Risk Committee.

## 4. Validation and monitoring
Pre-release: out-of-time test, stability tests, CI gate (`tests/test_quality_gate.py`).
Post-market monitoring: monthly performance report (AUC, Gini, default rate per score band), PSI
drift alerts, appeal reversal rate.

## 5. Incident reporting
Model incidents (wrong declines at scale, outages, discriminatory patterns) are logged in the
Operational Risk system within 24 hours and escalated to the Model Risk Committee; serious incidents
are reported to the AI Governance Board (ai-incidents@acme.example) and, where required, to the
competent authority.

# Model card: pd-lgbm-3.1.0

* **Owner:** Credit Risk Analytics (cra@acme-finance.example)
* **Type:** LightGBM binary classifier, probability of default within 12 months.
* **Intended use:** consumer personal-loan applications, EUR 1,000-75,000, EU retail customers.
* **Out of scope:** mortgages, business lending, collections prioritisation, fraud detection.
* **Training data:** 1.9M applications 2018-2023 with 12-month performance (`docs/data/training-data.md`).
* **Performance (out-of-time test 2024):** ROC-AUC 0.81, Gini 0.62, KS 0.47; calibration error 0.6 pp.
* **Fairness:** see `docs/fairness-report-2026Q2.md`.
* **Limitations:** thin-file applicants (no bureau history) have lower accuracy (AUC 0.72); not
  validated for applicants under 21.

# Training data: pd-lgbm-3.1.0

* **Origin:** ACME loan book 2018-2023 (1.9M applications) joined with 12-month repayment outcomes
  and bureau attributes at application time (contracted bureau, purpose: credit risk modelling).
* **Collection purpose:** creditworthiness assessment; model development is compatible further
  processing (assessment of 2024-01-10).
* **Preparation:** exclusion of fraud-flagged applications (0.8%); winsorisation of income at
  P99.5; missing bureau data imputed with a "thin file" indicator; reject inference via
  fuzzy augmentation for declined applications.
* **Splits:** train 2018-2022, validation 2023-H1, out-of-time test 2023-H2/2024.
* **Assumptions:** 90+ days past due within 12 months as default definition; macro conditions of
  2018-2023 representative for the next 2 years.
* **Known gaps:** few applicants under 21 and over 75; self-employed under-represented (6%).

# CreditLens architecture

```
Loan origination platform ──OAuth2──► API Gateway (throttling) ──► creditlens (EKS, 3 pods)
                                                                   ├─ scoring.py (LightGBM + TreeSHAP reason codes)
                                                                   ├─ audit.py  ──► CloudWatch /creditlens/audit
                                                                   ├─ underwriting_queue / appeals_queue (SQS)
                                                                   └─ S3 acme-creditlens-applications (KMS)
```

* The service is stateless; application records are written by origination to S3 `records/`.
* Underwriters work in the origination back office, which reads the SQS queues.
* Model artefacts are baked into the container image; version reported in every response.

dpo@acme-finance.example. Retention: 5 years (legal obligation). You can lodge a complaint with your
supervisory authority.

import hashlib

def audit_decision(app_in, result, decision, caller):

        "caller": caller.client_id,
    })


def audit_appeal_outcome(application_id, ticket, outcome, note, caller):
